questions.stem: Atropine is useful in organophosphate poisoning because it:

options.label: C
options.text: Binds with both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors

options.label: D
options.text: Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine

questions.answerText: Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine

 

  • Atropine is useful in organophosphate poisoning because it acts as a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors.
  • Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme responsible for breaking down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft. 
  • This leads to an excessive accumulation of acetylcholine, which overstimulates the muscarinic receptors throughout the body.
  • Atropine, as a competitive antagonist, binds to the muscarinic receptors and blocks the action of acetylcholine. 
  • By doing so, atropine helps to counteract the excessive stimulation of muscarinic receptors caused by the organophosphate poisoning. 
  • This can alleviate symptoms such as excessive salivation, bronchoconstriction, bradycardia, and gastrointestinal distress that result from excessive cholinergic activity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reactivates acetylcholine esterase: This statement is incorrect. Atropine does not reactivate acetylcholinesterase. Instead, it acts as a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, blocking the excessive stimulation caused by the inhibition of acetylcholinesterase. Oximes act by reactivating acetylcholine esterase.

 

Option B. Competes with acetylcholine release: This statement is also incorrect. Atropine does not compete with acetylcholine release. It acts on the postsynaptic receptors (muscarinic receptors) rather than affecting the release of acetylcholine.

 

Option C. Binds with both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors: This statement is also incorrect. While atropine primarily binds to muscarinic receptors, it has minimal affinity for nicotinic receptors. Its main action is on muscarinic receptors, blocking the effects of acetylcholine at these receptors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Atropine is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors and is used in organophosphate poisoning to reverse muscarinic symptoms. 
  • Pralidoxime is required to reactivate acetylcholinesterase and relieve nicotinic effects.

questions.stem: Which of the following effects of adrenaline would be blocked by phentolamine (alpha receptor blocker) but NOT by propranolol (beta receptor antagonist)?

options.label: A
options.text: Release of renin from JG cells

options.label: C
options.text: Tremors due to stimulation of muscle spindle

options.label: D
options.text: Contraction of the vascular smooth muscle

questions.answerText: Contraction of the vascular smooth muscle
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Contraction of the vascular smooth muscle

  • Phentolamine is an alpha adrenergic receptor antagonist, while propranolol is a non-selective beta adrenergic receptor antagonist. This means that phentolamine will block the effects of adrenaline that are mediated by alpha receptors, and propranolol will block effects mediated by beta receptors.
  • Let's review the effects of adrenaline and which receptors they act on:
    • Release of renin from JG cells: This is mediated by Beta-1 adrenergic receptors. Propranolol (a beta blocker) would block this effect, but phentolamine (an alpha blocker) would not.
    • Relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle: This is mediated by Beta-2 adrenergic receptors. Again, propranolol would block this, but phentolamine would not.
    • Tremors due to stimulation of muscle spindle: This is also mediated by Beta-2 adrenergic receptors. So, propranolol would block this effect, but phentolamine would not.
    • Contraction of the vascular smooth muscle: This effect of adrenaline is mediated primarily by Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Phentolamine, being an alpha receptor blocker, would block this effect, but propranolol, a beta receptor blocker, would not.
  • Therefore, the answer to this question is option d i.e. contraction of the vascular smooth muscle.


ore, the answer to this question is option d i.e. contraction of the vascular smooth muscle.

questions.stem: During your rural posting after the internship, you encounter a patient of acute cardiac failure. Your preferred drug for this condition is dobutamine. However, it is not available there. Which of the following other drugs, or combination of drugs, would be a suitable alternative, giving the pharmacologic equivalent of what you want the dobutamine to do?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Norepinephrine plus phentolamine

Dobutamine primarily stimulates beta-1 adrenergic receptors leading to increased myocardial contractility (positive inotropy) and slightly increased heart rate (positive chronotropy) with minimal effects on blood vessels (vasculature).

Among the options given:

a. Norepinephrine plus Phentolamine - Norepinephrine stimulates alpha 1, alpha 2 and beta 1 receptors whereas Phentolamine is a nonselective alpha-adrenergic antagonist that would block both alpha 1 and alpha 2 receptors. So, the net effect is stimulation of beta 1 receptors only. This combination thus produces the action similar to dobutamine.

b. Dopamine (at a very high dose) - Dopamine at high doses stimulates alpha-1, beta-1, and dopaminergic receptors. While the beta-1 effect may be beneficial similar to dobutamine, the alpha-1 adrenergic stimulation could increase afterload and thus is not an ideal substitute for dobutamine.

c. Ephedrine plus Propranolol - Ephedrine is a non-selective adrenergic agonist stimulating both alpha and beta receptors. Propranolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist. This combination result in stimulation of only alpha receptors and thus is not an ideal replacement for dobutamine.

d. Phenylephrine plus Atropine - Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that would increase vascular resistance (afterload) which could further compromise a failing heart. Atropine blocks the parasympathetic stimulation of the heart leading to an increase in heart rate but doesn't have a significant inotropic effect. Thus this combination cannot be used as a replacement of dobutamine.

The correct answer therefore would be combination of NA and phentolamine.



ore would be combination of NA and phentolamine.

questions.stem: An old patient Ravi, having asthma and glaucoma is to receive a β blocker. Regarding β blocking drugs:

options.label: B
options.text: Esmolol’s pharmacokinetics are compatible with chronic topical use

options.label: D
options.text: Timolol lacks the local anaesthetic effects of propranolol

questions.answerText: Timolol lacks the local anaesthetic effects of propranolol
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Timolol lacks the local anesthetic effects of propranolol

  • Regarding the statements about β-blocking drugs:
    • Metoprolol blocks β2 receptors selectively. False. Metoprolol is a selective β1 receptor blocker, meaning it primarily blocks β1 adrenergic receptors. It has limited activity on β2 receptors. Selective β blockers are preferred in patients with asthma to minimize bronchoconstriction.
    • Esmolol's pharmacokinetics are compatible with chronic topical use. False. Esmolol is primarily administered intravenously and has a very short half-life of about 9 minutes. It is not suitable for chronic topical use. Esmolol is typically used for acute intravenous treatment of conditions such as arrhythmias or intraoperative hypertension.
    • Nadolol lacks β2 blocking action. False. Nadolol is a non-selective β blocker, meaning it blocks both β1 and β2 adrenergic receptors. It has equal affinity for both receptor subtypes.
    • Timolol lacks the local anaesthetic effects of propranolol. True. Timolol is a non-selective β blocker and lacks the local anaesthetic effects seen with propranolol. Propranolol has additional membrane-stabilizing properties and local anaesthetic effects due to its sodium channel blocking activity, which are not present in timolol.
  • In summary, the correct statement among the given options is: c. Timolol lacks the local anaesthetic effects of propranolol.


erred in patients with asthma to minimize bronchoconstriction.

questions.stem: Jugal, a patient suffering from hypertension, was administered propranolol. While it successfully managed the hypertension, it unfortunately dropped his resting heart rate to 50 beats per minute. Which of the following β blockers can be used as a suitable replacement for propranolol in Jugal's case that wouldn't result in severe bradycardia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Pindolol

Pindolol is a β-adrenergic antagonist (β-blocker) that has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA). Unlike other β-blockers such as propranolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, and labetalol, pindolol can stimulate the β-adrenergic receptors while blocking the effects of adrenaline and other stimulating agents. This intrinsic activity helps to maintain a more normal heart rate while still exerting the blood pressure lowering effect. As a result, pindolol would be less likely to induce severe bradycardia in comparison to the other β-blockers listed in the options.

questions.stem: A patient receives bethanechol after abdominal surgery. Her heart rate falls slightly and she experiences some wheezing. Which of the following best explains these cardiac and pulmonary responses?

options.label: C
options.text: Patient has undiagnosed interstitial lung disease

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Expected side effects of bethanechol

  • Bethanechol is a parasympathomimetic drug that is used to increase the tone and contractions of the urinary bladder and gastrointestinal tract. It stimulates muscarinic receptors, leading to various effects including decreased heart rate (due to stimulation of the vagus nerve) and bronchoconstriction.
  • The decreased heart rate seen in this patient could be an expected side effect of bethanechol (option a), due to its stimulation of the parasympathetic nervous system which normally slows heart rate.
  • As for the wheezing, this could be related to bronchoconstriction, a possible side effect of bethanechol due to its action on muscarinic receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle. This might suggest a previously undiagnosed pulmonary condition. However, interstitial lung disease (option c) usually presents with a dry cough and shortness of breath rather than wheezing, which is more characteristic of obstructive airway diseases like asthma or COPD.
  • AV block (option b) primarily presents with heart rhythm disturbances and not with pulmonary symptoms.
  • In light of this, the best answer to this question would be:
    • Expected side effects of bethanechol.

questions.stem: After undergoing a comprehensive eye exam, a patient exits the ophthalmologist's office and steps into bright sunlight. The topical drug administered during the exam not only dilated the patient's pupils but also affected their ability to focus on nearby objects. Which of the following drugs is most similar in its effects to the one given to the patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Homatropine

The drug that works most similarly to the one given to the patient, which dilated their pupils and impaired their ability to focus up close, is b. Homatropine.

  • Homatropine is a medication commonly used in ophthalmology to dilate the pupils (mydriasis) and temporarily paralyze the muscles that control accommodation (cycloplegia). Cycloplegia refers to the inability to focus on nearby objects due to the paralysis of the ciliary muscle in the eye, which is responsible for changing the shape of the lens to allow for near vision.
  • Physostigmine, on the other hand, is a cholinesterase inhibitor that is used to reverse the effects of drugs with anticholinergic properties, including those that cause pupil dilation and impaired accommodation.
  • Pilocarpine is a medication that causes constriction of the pupil (miosis) and stimulates accommodation, therefore having effects opposite to those described in the question.
  • Donepezil is a medication commonly used to treat Alzheimer's disease by inhibiting the breakdown of acetylcholine. It may cause miosis due to its cholinergic action but it does not have the specific effects mentioned in the question.


ers to the inability to focus on nearby objects due to the paralysis of the ciliary muscle in the eye, which is responsible for changing the shape of the lens to allow for near vision.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman with diagnosed myasthenia gravis presents with profound skeletal muscle weakness. We are unsure whether she is experiencing a cholinergic crisis or a myasthenic crisis, so we administer a usually appropriate dose of parenteral edrophonium. Assume the patient was actually experiencing a cholinergic crisis. Which of the following is the most likely response to the drug?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypertensive crisis from peripheral vascular constriction

options.label: B
options.text: Myocardial ischemia, and angina, from drug-induced tachycardia and coronary vasoconstriction

options.label: C
options.text: Prompt improvement of skeletal muscle tone and function

options.label: D
options.text: Ventilatory distress or failure due to paralysis of respiratory muscles

questions.answerText: Ventilatory distress or failure due to paralysis of respiratory muscles
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Ventilatory distress or failure due to paralysis of respiratory muscles.

  • Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder characterized by weakness and rapid fatigue of muscles under voluntary control. Patients with this condition may experience a myasthenic crisis, which is a severe episode of muscle weakness due to less stimulation of Nm receptors, or a cholinergic crisis, which is a severe episode of muscle weakness due to overmedication with anticholinesterase drugs.
  • Edrophonium is a short-acting anticholinesterase drug often used as a diagnostic tool to differentiate between a myasthenic crisis and a cholinergic crisis. If a patient is experiencing a myasthenic crisis, administration of edrophonium will temporarily improve muscle strength and function, because the problem in this situation is a lack of sufficient acetylcholine activity at the neuromuscular junction.
  • However, if the patient is actually experiencing a cholinergic crisis due to overmedication with anticholinesterase drugs, then administration of additional edrophonium (another anticholinesterase) would be expected to exacerbate the symptoms by further increasing acetylcholine levels. This can lead to overstimulation of the muscles, including the muscles involved in respiration, potentially resulting in respiratory failure.
  • Therefore, if this patient were in a cholinergic crisis, the most likely response to edrophonium would be option d i.e. Ventilatory distress or failure due to paralysis of respiratory muscles.


ore, if this patient were in a cholinergic crisis, the most likely response to edrophonium would be option d i.e. Ventilatory distress or failure due to paralysis of respiratory muscles.

questions.stem: Neeraj, a farmer comes to you in the emergency in comatose state. Patient had profuse sweating and lacrimation. Diarrhea and urination were apparent. On examination pupil was constricted and BP of the farmer was 80/60 mm Hg. You make a diagnosis of anticholinesterase poisoning. You decide to administer him atropine. All of the following actions will be reversed by atropine EXCEPT:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Muscle paralysis

  • The farmer's symptoms, such as profuse sweating, lacrimation, constricted pupils, diarrhea, urination, and hypotension, are indicative of a cholinergic crisis often caused by anticholinesterase poisoning (such as from organophosphate pesticides). Anticholinesterase compounds inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, leading to an overabundance of acetylcholine, which stimulates the parasympathetic nervous system. This results in symptoms such as excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastric upset, and sweating (often remembered as the "SLUDGE" syndrome).
  • Atropine is a muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist. It works by blocking the effects of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, which are found in the heart, exocrine glands, smooth muscles, and the central nervous system.
  • Atropine can effectively reverse many of the symptoms caused by anticholinesterase poisoning, including diarrhea (by reducing gut motility), bronchoconstriction (by relaxing smooth muscles in the airways), and some of the central effects such as coma. However, atropine cannot reverse the effects of acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors, which are found at the neuromuscular junction and are responsible for skeletal muscle contraction. Therefore, it will not be able to counteract muscle paralysis.


ore, it will not be able to counteract muscle paralysis.

questions.stem: A patient has supraventricular tachycardia. We inject a drug and heart rate falls to a normal or at least more acceptable level. Although this drug caused the desired response, it did so without any direct effect on the heart. Which of the following drugs was most likely used?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Phenylephrine

  • The question mentions that the drug doesn't directly affect the heart, implying that it likely acts elsewhere to mediate a reflex change in heart rate.
  • Let's examine the provided options:
    • Metoprolol is a beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist (beta-blocker) that reduces heart rate and contractility by directly blocking beta-1 receptors in the heart.
    • Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist. It causes vasoconstriction, which can lead to reflex bradycardia due to activation of baroreceptors.
    • Prazosin is an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist primarily used for treating hypertension. It doesn't directly decrease heart rate, but rather it. May increase it due to reflex activation of sympathetic system.
    • Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist and increases heart rate by blocking the action of the parasympathetic nervous system on the heart.
  • Among these options, the drug that fits the description best, causing a decrease in heart rate without directly affecting the heart, is: b. Phenylephrine.


lex change in heart rate.

questions.stem: A substance abuser self-administers cocaine and experiences a variety of significant changes in cardiovascular function, in addition to the CNS-stimulating effects for which the drug is used. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism by which the cocaine causes its main peripheral effects?

options.label: A
options.text: Activation of α-2-adrenergic receptors leading to increased NA release

options.label: B
options.text: Blockage of NA reuptake via the amine pump

options.label: C
options.text: Direct activation of postsynaptic α-and –β adrenergic receptors

questions.answerText: Blockage of NA reuptake via the amine pump
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Blockage of NA reuptake via the amine pump

  • Cocaine's primary mechanism of action in the peripheral nervous system is to block the reuptake of monoamines, such as norepinephrine (NA), dopamine, and serotonin, by inhibiting the presynaptic transporters. This results in an increased concentration of these neurotransmitters in the synaptic cleft, leading to an amplified and prolonged signal at the postsynaptic receptors.
  • In terms of cardiovascular effects, the heightened norepinephrine (NA) activity at the sympathetic neuroeffector junctions leads to increased heart rate, blood pressure, and vasoconstriction. These effects can have harmful consequences, particularly in individuals with pre-existing cardiovascular conditions.

questions.stem: We administer an “effective” dose of a drug Y and observe the following responses:Stimulates the heartDilates some blood vessels but constricts noneDilates the bronchiRaises blood glucose levels in presence of hypoglycemiaNo effect on the size of the pupilDrug Y acts on which of the following receptors?

options.label: B
options.text: Agonist of all α and β-adrenergic receptors

options.label: C
options.text: Agonist of α1 and α2 receptors

options.label: D
options.text: Agonist of β1 and β2 receptors

questions.answerText: Agonist of β1 and β2 receptors
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Agonist of β1 and β2 receptors

 

  • Let's break down the effects:
    • Stimulates the heart: This is typically mediated by Beta-1 adrenergic receptors.
    • Dilates some blood vessels but constricts none: Vessel dilation is usually caused by Beta-2 adrenergic receptors. Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors generally cause constriction, but you noted there's no constriction.
    • Dilates the bronchi: Bronchodilation is typically mediated by Beta-2 adrenergic receptors.
    • Raises blood glucose levels in presence of hypoglycemia: This could be due to Beta-2 adrenergic receptors, which stimulate glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver.
    • No effect on the size of the pupil: This suggests the drug does not act on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, which would typically cause pupil dilation (mydriasis), or muscarinic receptors, which would cause pupil constriction (miosis).
  • Based on these responses, the drug Y likely acts as an agonist on Beta-1 and Beta-2 receptors.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be blocked by atropine?

options.label: A
options.text: Bradycardia caused by infusion of acetylcholine

options.label: B
options.text: Increased blood pressure caused by nicotine

options.label: C
options.text: Increased skeletal muscle strength caused by neostigmine

questions.answerText: Bradycardia caused by infusion of acetylcholine
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Bradycardia caused by infusion of acetylcholine

 

  • Atropine is an antimuscarinic agent, which works by blocking acetylcholine from binding to muscarinic receptors in the parasympathetic nervous system. However, it does not block the nicotinic receptors. 

    • Bradycardia caused by infusion of acetylcholine – This action is mediated by M2 receptors of Ach. Atropine can block this because it inhibits the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, which can slow heart rate.

    • Increased blood pressure caused by nicotine – Nicotine causes activation of sympathetic system by stimulating the nicotinic Nn receptors at ganglia. As atropine does not block nicotinic receptors, it cannot stop this action.

    • Increased skeletal muscle strength caused by neostigmine - Atropine would not block this effect. Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction, leading to increased muscle strength. This effect is primarily mediated by nicotinic Nm receptors. As atropine does not act on nicotinic receptors, so atropine would not directly counteract it.

questions.stem: A new drug has been found to act by inhibiting VMAT-2. Which of the following statement regarding this drug is likely to be TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Blocks both α and β receptor mediated effects of injected adrenaline

options.label: B
options.text: Does not block any effect of injected nor-adrenaline

options.label: C
options.text: Does not block the effects of sympathetic nerve Stimulation

questions.answerText: Does not block any effect of injected nor-adrenaline
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Does not block any effect of injected nor-adrenaline

  • VMAT-2, or Vesicular Monoamine Transporter 2, is a protein that transports neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and adrenaline (epinephrine) into synaptic vesicles for storage and later release.
  • So, a drug that inhibits VMAT-2 would reduce the storage and subsequent release of these neurotransmitters. This would not directly influence the receptor-mediated effects of these neurotransmitters once they have been released into the synaptic cleft. Therefore, this drug:
    • Would not block α and β receptor-mediated effects of injected adrenaline, because these effects are post-release, and the drug works by limiting the storage and release of neurotransmitters.
    • Would not block any effect of injected nor-adrenaline, again because this drug acts on the storage and release of neurotransmitters, not on their effects once they are in the synaptic cleft.
    • Would block the effects of sympathetic nerve stimulation, as the drug result in less storage of neurotransmitters in the vesicles and thus there will be less release of NA on sympathetic nerve stimulation.


ore, this drug:

questions.stem: A healthy adult subject is given an intravenous injection of a test drug. Both blood pressure and total peripheral resistance rise promptly. This is associated with a reduction of heart rate. In repeated experiments we find that the vasopressor response is not affected by pretreatment with prazosin (alpha blocker). However, pretreatment with atropine prevents the bardycardia. The test drug was most likely which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Angiotensin II

  • The question describes an agent that increases both blood pressure and total peripheral resistance, indicating a vasoconstrictor effect.
  • It also causes a reduction in heart rate, likely through a reflex mechanism in response to increased blood pressure (baroreceptor reflex).
  • The fact that prazosin (an alpha-blocker) does not affect the response suggests that the agent is not primarily acting through alpha adrenergic receptors, ruling out agents such as noradrenaline and adrenaline (norepinephrine).
  • However, the observation that atropine prevents the bradycardia suggests involvement of the parasympathetic nervous system, as atropine is a muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist.
  • Among the choices provided, angiotensin II fits this profile the best. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that can raise blood pressure and increase total peripheral resistance. Its effect on heart rate is less direct; the increase in blood pressure it causes can stimulate baroreceptor reflexes, leading to increased parasympathetic (vagal) outflow and resulting in a reduction in heart rate (bradycardia). This bradycardia could be blocked by atropine.

Its effect on heart rate is less direct; the increase in blood pressure it causes can stimulate baroreceptor reflexes, leading to increased parasympathetic (vagal) outflow and resulting in a reduction in heart rate (bradycardia). This bradycardia could be blocked by atropine.

questions.stem: Cholinomimetic drugs can be used for the treatment of all the following conditions except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Bradycardia

  • Cholinomimetic drugs, also known as parasympathomimetic drugs, are those that mimic the effects of acetylcholine, the primary neurotransmitter in the parasympathetic nervous system. They stimulate muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic receptors and are used in a variety of conditions:
    • Closed angle glaucoma: Cholinomimetics like pilocarpine cause constriction of the pupil (miosis), opening the angle in the eye and increasing the outflow of aqueous humor, thereby reducing intraocular pressure. They are indeed used in the treatment of acute closed-angle glaucoma.
    • Bradycardia: Bradycardia, or slow heart rate, is not typically treated with cholinomimetics. Rather, these agents could potentially worsen bradycardia since activation of muscarinic receptors in the heart (specifically the M2 subtype) would lead to decreased heart rate.
    • Cobra bite: Some cholinomimetics (e.g., neostigmine) can be used to combat the effects of a cobra bite. Cobra venom contains a neurotoxin that inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, leading to paralysis. Cholinomimetics can help overcome this paralysis.
    • Myasthenia gravis: Cholinomimetics such as pyridostigmine are used to treat myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disorder that causes weakness in the skeletal muscles. These drugs inhibit acetylcholinesterase and therefore increase the amount of acetylcholine available at the neuromuscular junction, helping to alleviate muscle weakness.


ore increase the amount of acetylcholine available at the neuromuscular junction, helping to alleviate muscle weakness.

questions.stem: A patient presents in the emergency department in great distress and with the following signs and symptoms: Mental confusion Clear lungs, no wheezing or crepitations High heart rate Absence of bowel sounds Distended abdomen Full bladder Hot, dry skin Absence of lacrimal, salivary secretions Very high fever Dilated pupils that do not respond to light Which of the following drug overdose is most likely to be responsible for these signs and symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Atropine

  • The symptoms listed in the question are indicative of a classic anticholinergic syndrome, which includes fever, flushing (hot, dry skin), blurred vision due to mydriasis (dilated pupils), altered mental status (confusion), urinary retention (full bladder), decreased bowel sounds (gut atony), and absence of lacrimal and salivary secretions (dry mouth and eyes).
  • Organophosphates and propranolol do not generally cause these symptoms.
  • Organophosphates, which are often used in pesticides and nerve gases, act as cholinergic agents by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase. This would lead to an overabundance of acetylcholine, causing a cholinergic crisis characterized by symptoms such as excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastric upset, and sweating (often remembered as the "SLUDGE" syndrome).
  • Propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker, can lead to bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, and potentially even heart failure in case of overdose, but would not typically cause the symptoms described here.
  • On the other hand, atropine, a muscarinic antagonist, inhibits the action of acetylcholine at the muscarinic receptors in the parasympathetic nervous system, causing an anticholinergic syndrome.

questions.stem: All of the following are features of atenolol in comparison to propranolol EXCEPT?

options.label: A
options.text: It is ineffective in suppressing muscle tremor

options.label: C
options.text: It is less likely to cause bradycardia

options.label: D
options.text: It is less likely to worsen Raynaud’s disease

questions.answerText: It is less likely to cause bradycardia
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. It is less likely to cause bradycardia

  • Atenolol and propranolol are both beta-blockers, but they have different selectivities. Atenolol is a selective beta-1 blocker, meaning it primarily affects beta-1 adrenergic receptors found mostly in the heart. Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker and blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, the latter of which are found in the lungs, blood vessels, and skeletal muscles.
  • Considering the options:
    • It is ineffective in suppressing muscle tremor: This is true. Propranolol can suppress muscle tremors because it blocks beta-2 adrenergic receptors found in the muscles. Atenolol, being a beta-1 selective blocker, does not have this effect.
    • It is safer in asthmatics: This is also true. Beta-2 adrenergic receptor blockade can lead to bronchoconstriction, which can be dangerous in patients with asthma. Because atenolol selectively blocks beta-1 receptors, it is safer for asthmatics than propranolol.
    • It is less likely to cause bradycardia: This statement is false. Both atenolol and propranolol, by virtue of blocking beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart, can cause bradycardia (slowing of the heart rate). Atenolol is not less likely to cause bradycardia compared to propranolol.
    • It is less likely to worsen Raynaud’s disease: True. Propranolol can exacerbate Raynaud's disease, a condition characterized by decreased blood flow to the extremities in response to cold or stress, due to its non-selective blockade of beta receptors, including those causing vasoconstriction in the skin (beta-2). Atenolol, with its selective beta-1 activity, is less likely to have this effect.
  • So, the statement that does not hold true when comparing atenolol with propranolol is option c i.e. It is less likely to cause bradycardia.

questions.stem: In general, structures that are affected by sympathetic activation respond to both sympathetic neural activation and to the hormonal component, adrenaline released from the adrenal medulla. Which of the following structures is unique in that it responds to adrenaline, but not nor-adrenaline?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Bronchus

  • Adrenaline activates all the sympathetic receptors including alpha 1, alpha 2, beta 1 and beta 2. Nor-adrenaline mainly acts on alpha 1, alpha 2 and beta 1 receptors. It has negligible action on beta 2 receptors.
  • The bronchus in the lungs contains predominantly beta-2 adrenergic receptors, which respond to adrenaline but not to noradrenaline.
  • When adrenaline binds to the beta-2 receptors in the bronchus, it induces bronchodilation – the widening of the bronchial air passages. This is part of the 'fight or flight' response initiated by the sympathetic nervous system, which enhances air flow and oxygen supply during situations that demand increased physical activity or alertness.
  • On the contrary, the atrioventricular node and renal juxtaglomerular apparatus contain beta 1 receptors that can be stimulated by both adrenaline as well as nor-adrenaline.
  • Iris of the eye contains alpha 1 receptors, these can also be stimulated by both adrenaline as well as nor-adrenaline.
  • Therefore, the bronchus is unique among the choices given in its selective response to adrenaline over noradrenaline.


ore, the bronchus is unique among the choices given in its selective response to adrenaline over noradrenaline.

questions.stem: A 28 yr old woman has been treated with several autonomic drugs for about a month. Which of the following signs would distinguish between an overdose of a muscarinic blocker and a ganglionic blocker?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Postural hypotension

  • Ganglionic blockers affect both the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous systems, since they block transmission through both types of autonomic ganglia. One of the effects of blocking sympathetic transmission would be to reduce vascular tone, leading to hypotension. When this occurs particularly upon standing up, it's known as postural (or orthostatic) hypotension.
  • Muscarinic blockers, on the other hand, primarily affect the parasympathetic nervous system, as most of the parasympathetic nerve endings release acetylcholine that acts on muscarinic receptors. Overdose of a muscarinic blocker can cause symptoms such as dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and mydriasis (dilation of the pupils), but it generally wouldn't cause postural hypotension as it doesn't impact the sympathetic control of vascular tone.
  • Therefore, postural hypotension can be a distinguishing sign of an overdose of a ganglionic blocker versus a muscarinic blocker.


ore, postural hypotension can be a distinguishing sign of an overdose of a ganglionic blocker versus a muscarinic blocker.
